author: Unknown
title: Bilgesu Erenus Nakkaştepe'de toprağa verildi
content:
5 Ağustos 2026 Çarşamba günü, 83 yaşında aramızdan ayrılan Erenus için ilk uğurlama töreni Harbiye Muhsin Ertuğrul Sahnesi'nde düzenlendi. Törene ailesi, yakınları, sanatçılar, tiyatro emekçileri ve çok sayıda seveni katıldı.


Bilgesu Erenus hayatını kaybetti


5 Ağustos 2026


Tören, Bilgesu Erenus'un yaşamı ve çalışmalarını anlatan kısa bir video gösterimiyle başladı.


İstanbul Şehir Tiyatroları Genel Sanat Yönetmeni Ayşegül İşsever, konuşmasında Erenus'un "yalnızca üretken bir sanatçı değil, toplumsal sorunlar karşısında sorumluluk üstlenen cesur bir aydın" olduğunu vurguladı. Erenus'un eserlerinin yeni kuşaklarla buluşmaya devam ettiğini belirten İşsever, özellikle 5 yıldır kapalı gişe sahnelenen Yaftalı Tabut oyununun sanatçının kalıcı mirasının önemli örneklerinden biri olduğunu söyledi.


Oğlu Ali Erenus ise annesini yaşamı boyunca ezilenlerin, emekçilerin ve hak arayanların yanında duran bir aydın olarak anlattı. Bilgesu Erenus'un hiçbir zaman kişisel çıkar uğruna ilkelerinden ödün vermediğini belirten Ali Erenus, sanatçının yalnızca eserleriyle değil, yaşamı ve duruşuyla da çok sayıda insana ilham verdiğini dile getirdi.


Toplumun aydınlarına onlar yaşarken sahip çıkılması gerektiğini vurgulayan Erenus, annesine "Bana sesi, sözü ve insanların ruhuna giden yolu aydınlatan ışığı verdin" sözleriyle veda etti.


Toplumcu sanat dünyasında iz bıraktı 


1943'te Bilecik'te doğan Bilgesu Erenus, tiyatro, sinema ve müzik alanlarında uzun yıllar çalıştı ve eser verdi. Eserlerinde ağırlıklı olarak emek ve emekçiler, toplumsal eşitsizlikler, kadınların yaşamı ve demokrasi mücadelesini ele aldı. Özellikle Yaftalı Tabut, Misafir ve çeşitli senaryo çalışmalarıyla toplumcu sanat geleneğinin ilgi çeken şahsiyetleri  arasında yer aldı.


Şair Müştak Erenus’un eşi ve müzisyen Ali Erenus’un annesi olan

Bilgesu Erenus

, Kadıköy Kız Koleji'nden mezun olduktan sonra, bir süre hukuk fakültesinde ve konservatuvarda eğitim aldıktan sonra İstanbul Üniversitesi Gazetecilik Enstitüsü'nü bitirdi. 


1965-1973 arasında TRT'de çalışan Erenus, tiyatro, roman ve öyküleriyle tanındı.


Toplumsal meseleleri, emek, göç, kadın ve insan haklarını sahneye taşıyan Erenus'un oyunları, Türkiye dışında da çeşitli tiyatrolarda sahnelendi ve farklı dillere çevrildi.


Kaleme aldığı oyunlar Devlet Tiyatroları, Ankara Sanat Tiyatrosu ve Dostlar Tiyatrosu gibi önemli topluluklar tarafından sahnelendi. 

Yaftalı Tabut

, Misafir, El Kapısı, Ortak, Kelaynaklar, Güneyli Bayan ve Acılar Şenliği en bilinen yapıtları arasındaydı. Halide, Böyle Bir Dünya, Göz, Gece ve Kırmızı Karaağaç da Erenus'un ilgi gören kitapları arasındaydı. 

Erenus, toplumsal etkinliklerde yaptığı konuşmaların yanı sıra, gitarı eşliğinde seslendiği şarkılarla da toplumsal muhalefetin ön saflarında yer aldı.

author: Unknown
title: Güneş panellerinin açıyla durmasının bir sebebi var
content:
Son yıllarda çatılarda, tarlalarda ve binaların cephelerinde sıkça karşılaştığımız güneş panelleri dikkatinizi çekmiş olabilir: Bu paneller hiçbir zaman yere tamamen paralel (düz) veya dik şekilde yerleştirilmez. Belirli bir eğimle monte edilen panellerin bu duruşu yalnızca mimari bir tercih değil; arkasında fizik, coğrafya ve mühendislik kurallarının yattığı kritik bir hesaplamaya dayanıyor.

Güneş enerjisi sistemlerinin temeli, güneşten gelen fotonların panellere dik açıya yakın bir şekilde temas etmesine dayanır. Güneş ışınları bir yüzeye ne kadar dik (90 derece) vurursa, birim alana düşen enerji miktarı ve buna bağlı olarak üretilen elektrik o kadar yüksek olur.

Dünya’nın eksen eğikliği ve küresel yapısı nedeniyle güneş ışınları yeryüzüne hiçbir zaman tamamen dik bir açıyla sabit kalmaz. Panelleri belirli bir açıyla eğmek, gün içinde ve mevsimler boyunca gelen ışınları mümkün olan en dik açıya yaklaştırır.

Bir bölgedeki ideal panel açısı doğrudan o bölgenin coğrafi enlemine bağlıdır. Örneğin, Ekvator'a yakın bölgelerde paneller neredeyse düz sayılabilecek kadar düşük açılarla yerleştirilirken, kutuplara doğru gidildikçe panellerin eğim açısı belirgin şekilde artar. Türkiye gibi orta kuşak ülkelerinde ise paneller genellikle 30 ila 35 derece arasında bir eğimle monte edilir.

Güneş kış aylarında gökyüzünde daha alçak bir yörünge izlerken, yaz aylarında yükselir. Sabit panellerde bu durum göz önüne alınarak yıllık ortalama en yüksek verimi sağlayacak açı optimize edilir.

Panellerin eğimli olmasının son derece pratik ve biyolojik/çevresel bir nedeni daha vardır: Temizlik.

Tamamen düz yerleştirilen panellerin üzerinde yağmur suyu birikir; toz, polen, kuş pislikleri ve yapraklar panel yüzeyinde çamur tabakası oluşturur. Belirli bir eğim (genellikle en az 10–15 derece) sayesinde yağmur suları paneller üzerinden kayarak akar ve biriken tozu yıkayıp götürür. Temiz bir panel, kirli bir panele göre yüzde 15 ila yüzde 25 daha fazla enerji üretir.

Kış aylarında panellerin üzerinde biriken kar, hücrelerin güneşle temasını keserek elektrik üretimini tamamen durdurabilir. Eğimli panellerde kar kütlesi yerçekiminin etkisiyle kayarak dökülür. Ayrıca, birden fazla panel dizisinin bulunduğu santral sahalarında ön sıradaki panellerin arka sıradakileri gölgelemesini engellemek için ideal açı hesaplamaları hayati önem taşır.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Anna Maria Barry-Jester
title: Trump’s Foreign Aid Priority? Investigating Crime Against White South Africans
content:
Other proposed grant recipients include a British organization fighting to keep gay conversion therapy legal.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Since he returned to office, President Donald Trump’s administration has upended foreign aid. It’s labeled well-established, long-running programs as “ not aligned with American interests ” and slashed their budgets.

Still, the billions of taxpayer dollars Congress has allocated for foreign aid programs must be spent; lawmakers have insisted the government continue to fund humanitarian aid, global health and pro-democracy causes around the world. With most of the old programs now gone, however, we wanted to know: What is the Trump administration doing with that money now?

Recently, we published our investigation that found one answer to that question in a little-known bureau of the State Department that has dramatically transformed under Trump. For decades, the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor, known as DRL, has supported  human rights in some of the most oppressive countries in the world. Now, our reporting found,  it’s planning to direct funds to controversial groups supporting right-wing causes in Europe and elsewhere.

Our full story lays out some of the groups the government has considered funding, which include a British free-speech organization that has fought against bans on “gay conversion therapy” and a British American think tank created this year to focus on “existential threats to Britain, to America, and to our shared Judeo-Christian civilisation.” (Administration officials dropped that grant after significant pushback from Congress.)

One proposed grant particularly caught our attention: Trump administration officials suggested funding research on crime against minority populations in South Africa.

It’s clear from sources we spoke with that the key targeted minority population in question is the white ethnic group known as Afrikaners. Afrikaners were responsible for creating the nation’s infamous and brutal racially segregated apartheid system. Previously, DRL staff had been told to begin the process of awarding funds to a group called Lex Libertas, which was founded by a controversial figure who has called for Afrikaner self-governance . The group is currently fundraising to place 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall in remembrance of attacks on South African farmers.

The proposed grant was later opened up to allow a broader set of invited groups to apply for $1 million of funding, though it is still intended for the same purpose, according to people with knowledge of the process. The State Department declined to say whether Lex Libertas will be among those invited to compete, citing ongoing deliberations, but said the Trump administration has serious concerns about the human rights situation in South Africa that need to be addressed. Lex Libertas did not respond to questions about the organization or the proposed grant.

Former diplomats who have worked extensively on human rights told us they were shocked that the victimization of white South Africans would be prioritized over the serious issues elsewhere in the region.

“It’s laughable to suggest that on the African continent, the prime issue of human rights concern is whites in South Africa,” one former agency official said when we asked him about the grant. South Africa is plagued by violence, but extensive research has found that white South African farmers are not victims of crime at higher rates than other groups.

Experts also described the proposed grant to fund research into violence against Afrikaners as keeping with the Trump administration’s overall stance toward South Africa.

For decades, the U.S. relationship with the country has been symbolized by our massive support for HIV care, Mattie Webb, a professor at the Virginia Military Institute who studies South Africa and U.S. foreign policy, told us.

Since Trump returned to office, there’s been a stark shift as the administration has strengthened ties with borderline white nationalist groups that are considered fringe in South Africa.

“The U.S. is very clearly shifting its priorities away from aid that would benefit far more people in South Africa to this narrow focus on the white minority,” Webb said.

author: Candice Norwood
title: With Blanche Confirmed as AG, Epstein Survivors Say DOJ Continues to Fail Them
content:
“We have tried countless times to engage the DOJ, and they’ve had absolutely no interest,” said one survivor.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Every minute of every day, Liz Stein has to relive the worst thing that’s ever happened to her. She does it during news interviews and when meeting lawmakers on Capitol Hill to demand justice for herself and other survivors of the late disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

And she’s had to do it throughout the attorney general confirmation process for Todd Blanche , a man who rose from being President Donald Trump’s criminal defense lawyer to the top official overseeing the U.S. Department of Justice. Blanche has served as deputy attorney general, the No. 2 at DOJ, since March 2025. He then became acting attorney general in April after Trump fired his predecessor , Pam Bondi, and officially nominated him to oversee the department in June.

Since that time, Stein and her fellow survivors have consistently urged senators to vote against Blanche’s confirmation, arguing that he has shown no urgency or concern with expanding the Epstein investigation. Despite some initial pushback from two Republican members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Blanche cleared that first hurdle to advance to a full Senate vote, in part by meeting with survivors — something he’d previously declined to do.

Republican Sens. Susan Collins, who is in a tough re-election race in Maine, and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska then announced that they would join Democrats in voting against Blanche, raising the tension heading into the final vote. With last-minute support from GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the Senate confirmed Blanche, 50-49, early Saturday morning.

Stein told The 19th that just last year she felt momentum toward accountability growing, driven by public outrage from across the political spectrum and the Epstein survivors’ decision to step into the national spotlight as a unified group calling for transparency. However, Blanche’s confirmation crystalizes another feeling for Stein: “It feels like the DOJ is weaponizing this case for political reasons, and it feels like we’re the pawns being used in that game,” she told The 19th .

That momentum feels stagnant for now, Stein said, but she wants people to know that it won’t be a deterrent. “I think that every attempt the Department of Justice has made to make us go away has not worked,” she said. “We’re not going away.”

The Epstein cloud has hung over the Trump administration since the president began his second term, and included a series of perceived missteps by Bondi that drew criticism from both Democrats and Trump’s base.

In February 2025, Bondi claimed in interviews that her office would be releasing new documents tied to Epstein that would make people feel “sick,” and stated that she had a list of Epstein’s clients sitting on her desk. At a White House meeting the same month, she handed out binders to a group of right-wing social media influencers that contained no new information.

By July 2025, DOJ had released a memo stating it “did not uncover evidence that could predicate an investigation against uncharged third parties.” Trump supporters began to weigh in. Podcaster Joe Rogan, who boasts an average of about 11 million listeners and viewers per episode, accused the administration of “trying to gaslight” the public about how much information it had on the Epstein case.

For Stein, DOJ’s “nothing to see here” attitude has been a constant. In September 2025, the human trafficking specialist and a group of about a dozen other survivors gathered publicly for the first time, standing in front of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. They called for investigations into Epstein’s associates, no presidential pardons or concessions for Maxwell and a full release of the Epstein files — documents and images capturing his personal relationships, business dealings and crimes.

Survivors advocated for the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which became law in November 2025, and required the department to publish unclassified records and communications related to the investigation and prosecution of Epstein. Between December 2025 and March 2026, the department released hundreds of thousands of documents, photos and videos tied to Epstein.

author: Unknown
title: “I don’t want to die without seeing peace”
content:
When the hamlet of Birezayna, near the village of Temiran (Demirli), was burned down in the 1990s, İhsan Bayram and the other residents were forced to watch. Turkish soldiers lined up the villagers and made them witness the destruction of their homes. More than three decades later, the now 85-year-old man has returned to live in his village. He has lost much; family members, his homeland, and countless years of his life. Yet one wish remains: to live long enough to see peace.


“Every day I think about peace and about the return of those who were forced to leave,” Bayram said. “I hope I live long enough to see those days.”


A life in the shadow of war and displacement


İhsan Bayram’s story reflects the experience of many families in Kurdistan. Fifteen members of his extended family joined the PKK and lost their lives. Four other relatives, including his son, are currently in prison. One of his nephews was the victim of a political murder that remains unsolved to this day.


Bayram himself also spent 15 months in prison. In 2008, he was arrested along with numerous relatives following an explosion. While he was later released, his son Neytullah Bayram and his nephew Murat Yıldeniz were convicted in the same case and sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment. Yet, according to Bayram, his most painful memories go back much further.


“They brought me home every day and came back for me the next morning”


Bayram recalls that before the 1990s, his family made a living from livestock farming. There was a shortage of water, he said, but not of security. That changed completely with the escalation of the conflict in Kurdistan.


“They labeled us as terrorists. Altogether, I spent about seventy days in detention and was tortured. Every day they brought me back home, and the next morning they came to take me away again. Over and over. They did everything forcing us to abandon our village.”


In addition to torture, the villagers were subjected to threats and extrajudicial killings, Bayram said. He himself narrowly escaped death on several occasions.


“They wanted to kill me. Instead, after torturing me, they left me lying in front of my house until they came back again.”


When the village went up in flames


Eventually, Birezayna was destroyed. Bayram still vividly remembers the day when the villagers were forced to watch the destruction of their homes.


“They lined us all up and burned our houses before our eyes. Anyone who spoke was threatened with death. Columns of smoke were rising from villages everywhere.”


In the spring of 1994, the residents were loaded onto tractors and forcibly displaced—first to nearby villages and later to the city.


Alone in a destroyed village


Not long afterward, Bayram returned. Very little of his village remained. For three years, he lived there alone—without electricity, with almost no infrastructure, and surrounded by the ruins of the burned homes.


He was later displaced once again and relocated to the village of Seyrek, but he did not stay there.


“I couldn’t live anywhere else. This was my homeland.”


When Bayram eventually returned to Birezayna permanently, other families gradually followed. Slowly, the village began to come back to life. Even today, however, it still lacks basic infrastructure and public services. Electricity has since been restored, but access to water and roads remains a major problem.


“We are not asking for an apology, we are asking for peace”


Despite everything he has endured, Bayram says he remains hopeful about the current Peace and Democratic Society Process.


“Of course, I still have concerns. But if the state also does its part, then we can truly speak of peace.”


He says that people in the villages have paid a heavy price.


“We lost our children. We lost our property. We were driven from our homeland. Yet today we are not saying, ‘Apologize to us.’ We are saying, ‘Take a step toward peace.’ No more people should die.”


“I hope I live long enough to see those days”


At the age of 85, Bayram is focused less on the past than on what the future might bring.


“For decades, I have lived with the hope of peace. So much blood has been shed, so much suffering has taken place. This process must end in peace.”


He is especially moved by the thought of those who remain far from their homeland or are still in prison.


“I dream of the day when the guerrillas return and the prisoners are released. Every day I ask myself: Will I live to see that …

author: Brett Wilkins
title: New Mexico Court Fines Meta $567 Million for Harming Kids
content:
The company’s total fines for exposing children to exploitation and harming their mental health now top $1 billion.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

A New Mexico court on Thursday ruled that Meta must pay an additional $567 million fine on top of the $375 million a jury fined the tech giant in March for harms caused to teens and children who use its Instagram and Facebook social media platforms.

First Judicial District Judge Bryan Biedscheid said in his 68-pager ruling that “significant numbers of people in New Mexico experience harm from Meta’s products due to risks of sexual exploitation, interference with education, and adverse mental health outcomes.”

“The harm to the impacted New Mexicans is not doubtful, eventual, or contingent, but an immediate, temporally connected, and highly probable result of Meta’s actions,” he continued.

“The youth mental health crisis has inflicted significant and widespread harm in New Mexico in terms of the number of youth suffering mental health harms, the profound suffering they and those in their families suffer, and the resulting interferences with the functioning of the schools, law enforcement, [and] healthcare systems in New Mexico,” the judge added.

The case centered on allegations that Meta knowingly designed and operated Facebook and Instagram in ways that exposed children to harmful content, encouraged excessive use, and failed to adequately protect minors from exploitation. New Mexico officials argued that internal company knowledge and outside warnings showed Meta was aware of risks associated with its platforms but did not act sufficiently to address them.

Most of the new fine — $420 million — will go toward funding youth treatment services, while the rest is designated for awareness and prevention, screening services, and other costs.

Biedscheid’s order also compels Meta to make changes to its platforms in New Mexico, including removing “like” counts and only showing them to minors with parental consent, and prohibiting overnight push notifications for users under age 18.

“Regardless of whether it is labeled as an ‘addiction’ or ‘problematic use,’ the evidence at trial proved that design elements, such as autoplay, infinite scroll, ‘like counts,’ and push notifications create a product that, particularly for adolescent users, is highly rewarding psychologically and neurochemically,” he wrote. “As a result, for many, it is irresistibly compelling to start scrolling and very difficult to stop or abstain from its use.”

“In addition,” the judge added, “algorithmic content recommendations can create harmful feedback loops and ‘rabbit hole’ users. Within a similar vein, ‘like counts’… can provide a potentially harmful focus for adolescent users.”

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said the company would appeal the ruling, claiming: “We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.”

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez hailed the ruling, saying that “Meta built products it knew would fuel addiction, deepen a youth mental health crisis, and expose children to sexual exploitation, then lied to parents and policymakers about the danger. Today, it pays for that choice.”

At Fairplay — a children’s advocacy group — executive director Josh Golin hailed the “landmark ruling” as “the clearest indication yet that the tide is turning when it comes to protecting kids from social media.”

“For the first time, Meta is being compelled by a court to change its dangerous and harmful design,” he continued. “And with so many states lined up to sue Meta and other social media companies, we should expect to see a lot more injunctive relief to make online platforms used by young people safer.”

“This ruling also clearly indicates why families need the Kids Online Safety Act,” Golin added, referring to a controversial bill advanced this week by the Senate Commerce Committee. “The judge said it was up to Congress to address the addictive features on Instagram and other social media platforms. KOSA’s duty of care against compulsive use is the key to ensuring that Meta and other social media companies stop designing for addiction …

title: Bundestag Vice President calls for amnesty for Kurdish activists in Germany
content:
As the peace process between Turkey and the Kurdish PKK is gradually moving forward, German Parliament (Bundestag) Vice President Bodo Ramelow of the Left Party, believes that Germany can also contribute to the process. He calls on the German federal government to introduce an amnesty for Kurdish activists in Germany.


Speaking to

Rheinische Post

, Ramelow said: “The framework law on the peace process, which has now been submitted to the parliament in Ankara, opens new paths toward peace and is a response to the voluntary dissolution of the Kurdish PKK last year.”


He added: “The German federal government should support this process through diplomatic means and must now, just as Turkey intends to do, implement broad and swift amnesty measures for Kurdish activists in Germany.”


Under an amnesty, the state waives the prosecution or punishment of certain offenses. In Ramelow’s view, such a step would represent “a concrete contribution to peace in the region and to safeguarding Kurdish rights and interests.”


The call comes in response to a

framework law

 submitted to parliament by Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP). One of the bill’s stated objectives is to facilitate the reintegration of PKK members into civilian life in Turkey. It also seeks to establish a legal framework for the possible release of convicted PKK members.


“I welcome the fact that the Turkish government now appears ready to take concrete steps toward peace with the Kurdish people in Turkey,” Ramelow said. “It once again underscores the determination of the Kurdish population in Turkey to achieve democratic change and bring the country’s violent past to a definitive end.”

title: Iraqi Islamic Resistance: Decision to halt attacks is temporary
content:
Abu Alaa al-Walaei, Secretary-General of the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades, issued a statement regarding the Iraqi Resistance Front’s (Iraqi Islamic Resistance) decision to suspend attacks against Saudi Arabia.


Al-Walaei said that the Iraqi Islamic Resistance’s decision to halt attacks on Saudi Arabia is temporary. He explained that the decision was made at the request of leaders of the Coordination Framework, particularly Hadi al-Amiri, Secretary-General of the Badr Organization.

title: Figen Yüksekdağ’dan çerçeve yasa açıklaması: “Özgürlüğümüz için çerçeve yasaya gerek yok, ama tarihi bir anlamı var”
content:
Eski HDP Eş Genel Başkanı Figen Yüksekdağ, “Benim hakkımda da Selahattin Demirtaş hakkında da AİHM kararları var. Çerçeve yasaya gerek yok ki bizim özgürlüğümüz için. Ama bu yasanın haksız yere cezaevinde tutulan siyasi mahpusların tahliyesinden çok daha büyük ve tarihi bir anlamı var" şeklinde konuştu.

İlke TV Genel Yayın Yönetmeni Sevda Çetinkaya, Kocaeli 1 No'lu F Tipi Yüksek Güvenlikli Kapalı Ceza İnfaz Kurumunda görüştüğü Figen Yüksekdağ'ın söylediklerini aktardı.

Yüksekdağ, gelinen aşamanın kendiliğinden ortaya çıkmadığını; arkasında çok büyük bedeller ödenmiş bir mücadele olduğunu söyledi. Yüksekdağ, “Adı çerçeve ama dar bir çerçeve. Kim istemez bunun daha geniş, daha kapsayıcı olmasını? Dün geçti elime metin ve okuduğumda ‘yine güvenlik kaygısıyla yazılmış bir metinle karşı karşıyayım’ dedim. Suç ve ceza kavramlarının içinden barışa yol arayan bir metin. Asla unutulmaması gereken bir şey var ama. Kürt meselesi Türkiye’de ilk kez doğrudan bir yasal düzenlemenin konusu haline geldi, tarihi bir eşik bu. 1921 Anayasası belgeleri ve o dönem Kürtleri inkar etmeyen anlayışın terk edilmesinden 100 yıl sonra bugün Kürtleri hukuk içine almanın yolunu açacak bir yasal bir düzenlemeyi konuşuyoruz” dedi.

Yüksekdağ, Demirtaş'ın ve kendisinin tahliye edilme olanağına ilişkin ise şunları söyledi: “Bizler zaten haksız ve hukuksuz yere içerdeyiz siyasi faaliyetlerimizden yargılandık ve ceza aldık. Benim hakkımda da Selahattin Demirtaş hakkında da AİHM kararları var. Çerçeve yasaya gerek yok ki bizim özgürlüğümüz için. Ama bu çerçeve yasanın benim de Selahattin beyin de haksız yere cezaevinde tutulan siyasi mahpusların tahliyesinden çok daha büyük ve tarihi bir anlamı var.”

author: Randi Beers
title: News Quiz Aug. 8 | Jump into the water
content:
Happy August! Are you reading beyond the headlines? Read on to find out.


1.

 Iqaluit city council voted last week to give free Aquatic Centre passes to 10 cancer patients. Why?


A.

 A group of youths was behind the initiative, saying they wanted to create a non-profit that spreads random acts of kindness across the city.


B.

 A pair of doctors at Qikiqtani General Hospital plans to incorporate exercise into their patients’ treatment plans, based on research that shows structured activity helps fight cancer.


C.

 Administration identified a surprise surplus of money, and council voted this would be a nice thing to do with it.


2.

 Why might people in Iqaluit be seeing RCMP on more ATVs this summer?


A.

 Officers asked for them because they are fun to ride.


B.

 It’s a new community initiative to spread safety awareness, and it also helps police get to areas they can’t access with a police cruiser.


C.

 The federal government paid for a fleet of ATVs for V Division, so they need to get used.


3.

 Photos will be on their way to Kugaaruk soon. What is significant about them?


A.

 They are part of aerial surveys of areas that have never been seen from this vantage point.


B.

 They are some of the first photos ever taken in Kugaaruk.


C.

 The photos depict traditional life in the area before a community was incorporated at Pelly Bay.


4.

 The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. released its most recent northern housing report last week. What proportion of their salaries are Iqaluit’s Inuit population putting towards a new mortgage, on average, in 2025?


A.

 60 per cent


B.

 65 per cent


C.

 70 per cent


5.

 Those walking down Ottawa’s Arts Corridor might notice a giant reproduction of a Sedna embroidery hanging along the route. The piece reinterprets the story of Sedna, but how so?


A.

 It retells the tale through a feminist lens.


B.

 Sedna’s story is retold as though she were a millennial living in modern, urban Canada.


C.

 The embroidery reinterprets her story as though she were not a monster, but misunderstood.


Answers:


An unidentified child and an adult peek into a seal’s breathing hole. (Photo courtesy of Jim Miller)


1.

 B — Structured exercise for colorectal cancer patients has been shown to lead to a 37 per cent lower risk of death and a 28 per cent lower risk of recurrence or developing other cancers, so two doctors at Qikiqtani General Hospital in Iqaluit are incorporating it as part of the treatment plan for 10 patients.


2.

 B — Although ATVs are legitimately more fun to drive than a traditional vehicle, that’s not why police are on them this summer. RCMP officers are using the ATVs to spread safety awareness about the vehicles, get closer to the community and access places they can’t get to in a traditional police cruiser.


3.

 C — Many of the photos show members of Kugaaruk’s Immingark family living a traditional life in the mid 1960s. Lucy Immingark is expected to receive them soon and plans to display them in the hamlet. She said the photos are significant to her because they show her father, her grandfather and many other people she grew up with.


4.

 C — Inuit in Iqaluit put aside a whopping 70 per cent of their household income towards a new mortgage in 2025, according to research released last week by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp.


5.

 A — A giant replica of Gayle Uyagaqi Kabloona’s Sedna embroidery tells the sea monster’s tale through a feminist lens. She told Nunatsiaq News she wanted to tell a traditional story but examine women’s experiences as well. “As I got older, I noticed that a lot of the women in the traditional stories have some kind of violence done to them by the men in society, or their families, or their husbands, or somebody,” she said.

title: Kosova Başbakanı Kurti'ye mecliste yumurta fırlatıldı
content:
Fotoğraf: Xavier Lejeune/Wikimedia Commons CC BY 4.0

Kosova Başbakanı Albin Kurti'ye Meclis Genel Kurulunda Kosova'nın Geleceği İçin İttifak (AAK) Partisi Milletvekili Time Kadrijaj tarafından protesto amacıyla yumurta atıldı.

7 Haziran'daki erken genel seçimlerin sonuçlarının kesinleşmesinin ardından Kosova Meclisinin yeni başkanı ile yardımcılarını seçmek üzere genel kurul toplandı.

Seçimden birinci çıkan Kendin Karar Al Hareketi'nin (Vetevendosje) Genel Başkanı ve Başbakan Kurti, kürsüde yaptığı konuşmada, diğer siyasi partilerle kurumların oluşturulmasına ilişkin koalisyon görüşmelerinin sürdüğünü belirtti.

Yeni meclis başkanı adayını sunmayan ve görüşmeler için daha fazla zaman talep eden Kurti'nin bu tutumu, diğer siyasi partilerin tepkisine yol açtı. Partiler, Kurti'nin anayasaya aykırı davrandığını öne sürdü.

AAK Milletvekili Kadrijaj, kürsüdeki konuşmasını tamamlayan Kurti'nin yanına giderek çantasından çıkardığı yumurtaları protesto amacıyla fırlattı.

Olayın ardından milletvekilleri arasında kısa süreli gerginlik yaşandı, Meclis Başkanı seçimi için düzenlenen oturum ertelendi.

Kurti, yaptığı açıklamada, yumurtalı protestonun, "diğer partilerle görüşebilmek için ödemesi gereken bir bedelse bunu ödemeye hazır olduğunu" belirtti.

Kosova'da 9 Şubat 2025'te genel seçim, 28 Aralık 2025'te de erken genel seçim düzenlenmişti. Albin Kurti liderliğindeki hükümet, 11 Şubat'ta Meclisten güvenoyu almıştı.

Eski Kosova Cumhurbaşkanı Vjosa Osmani, 5 yıllık görev süresinin sona ermesinin ardından 4 Nisan'da görevini geçici olarak Kosova Meclis Başkanı Albulena Haxhiu'ya devretmişti.

Kosova Meclisi, milletvekillerinin yeni cumhurbaşkanını anayasanın öngördüğü süre içinde seçememesi nedeniyle 29 Nisan'da feshedilmiş, ülkede 7 Haziran'da bir kez daha erken genel seçim yapılmıştı. Meclisin yeni cumhurbaşkanını seçmekte yine başarısız olması halinde ülke, bir kez daha erken genel seçime gidebilir.

title: Journalist Deniz Fırat remembered on the twelfth anniversary of her martyrdom
content:
Leyla Yıldıztan, who was born in 1984 in Xecîxatun village in Çaldıran district of Van province, was known as Deniz Fırat in the PKK ranks. Since her village was located on the border between Turkey and Iran, her family was repeatedly subject to attacks. For this reason, her family moved to Maku in 1990 and then to Urmia in Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan, Iran). After a while, they settled in Xakûrkê in southern Kurdistan (northern Iraq).


Deniz, who stayed in Xakûrkê in 1991-1992, witnessed the attacks on Southern Kurdistan with the co-operation of the Turkish state and the ruling party, KDP. In this process, Deniz and her sister Sarya (Sakine Yıldıztan), influenced by the martyrdom of Bêrîtan (Gülnaz Karataş) who rejected the KDP's betrayal and chose resistance, decided to join the PKK. Her sister Binewş (Ayfer Yıldıztan), who had joined the PKK before Deniz, was martyred in a clash in Zap in 1997. Deniz only heard about the martyrdom of his sister Sarya, with whom she had joined the struggle, two years later, on 8 August 1999. Deniz was active in many areas in the guerrilla ranks and started to take part in press and media activities in 2007.


Starting her career in the press with the magazine "Tanrıça Zilan" [Zilan the Goddess], she also worked for the "Dengê Welat" [Voice of Homeland] radio. Later, in Maxmur Camp, she reported news for "Rojeva Welat" newspaper and various TV channels and agencies. She also wrote articles for the magazine "Zilan the Goddess". As a revolutionary journalist, she closely followed the attacks launched by ISIS against Maxmur on 6 August and lost her life on 8 August 2014.


On the twelfth anniversary of her martyrdom, Deniz Fırat was commemorated at her grave in the rural neighborhood of Xeçxatun in Van’s Çaldıran district.


In addition to her family, those attending the commemoration included representatives of the Mesopotamian Women Journalists Association (MKG), the Van branches of the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG), the Association for Solidarity, Unity, Culture and Mutual Assistance with Families Who Lost Their Relatives in the Cradle of Civilizations (MEBYA-DER), members of the Peace Mothers Assembly, district executives of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), and numerous journalists.


Ceylan Şahinli, a member of the MKG Van branch, said: “Like those who followed in her footsteps, Deniz Fırat carried on the tradition she came from. At a time when the whole world feared ISIS, she fought with her camera. Just like those who paid the price in the struggle for truth, she too gave her life for this cause.”


Deniz Fırat’s brother, Seyat Yıldıztan, said: “Deniz is not only our martyr but also the martyr of her party and her people. She fought with her camera, not for herself or for her family, but for all her people.”


DEM Party Çaldıran District Co-Chair Abbas Aksak also spoke, saying: “When the Kurdish people were attacked by ISIS, Deniz worked with her camera and her pen, reporting on the attacks for the entire world to see. She continued her struggle until the day she was martyred on August 8. She is a martyr of Kurdistan and of the free press.”


The commemoration concluded with participants placing flowers on her grave.

author: Unknown
title: Iraqi Chief of Staff visits Kirkuk
content:
Iraqi Chief of Staff Abdul Amir Yarallah arrived in Kirkuk accompanied by a high-ranking military delegation. During his visit, Yarallah is expected to hold a series of meetings with military commanders in the city.


According to reports, the discussions will focus on the dissolution of the West of the Tigris Operations Command and proposed organizational changes within the Kirkuk Operations Command.


The West of the Tigris Operations Command was responsible for security in the areas between Kirkuk and Salahaddin provinces, covering the region from the district of Dakuk to Tuz Khurmatu.


The Iraqi Chief of Staff’s visit to Kirkuk comes after Arshad Salihi, head of the Iraqi Turkmen Front in Kirkuk, called for federal forces to maintain their presence in the city.


Salihi argued that if the federal forces were to withdraw from the region, other forces could move in and create new problems.


According to reports, Salihi’s reference to “other forces” was understood to mean the Peshmerga forces.

author: thecollective
title: Announcing new counter-information website Belly of the Beast
content:
by

thecollective


Aug 8, 2026


From

Belly of the Beast


welcome to the belly of the beast, a counter-info site for anarchists and militants within the heart of empire in so-called california and the occupied western region beyond. this is a space to share explicitly anti-colonial, anti-capitalist, anti-patriarchal, anti-racist, and anti-fascist direct actions, communiques, analysis, and zines. we invite those that emanate with a passion for attack to share discussions on targets, tactics, operational security, recipes for destruction, and other incendiary and seductive remarks.


we are in the midst of a social war that has been ongoing for millennia and is boiling over into every crevice of this earth. our daily engagements are inescapably interlinked within an archaic leviathan that endlessly seeks to capture and enclose our every movement. these are dark times, yet we are insatiably compelled towards autonomy, a poetry evolving before our very eyes. there is always an ever blooming field, a cacophony of insurgent desire, a chaotic moshpit for those that seek a life of feral joy, that long to fulfill their visions of revolt and revel in the glory of an undomesticated life. this is a space for dreamers and lovers, haters and nihilists, thieves of the night and those that tend to the sun and lines of flight. sleep now by the fire and listen to the gentle yet voracious spread of the rhizomatic knowledge needed to undermine and attack the last vestiges of a decaying empire.


like dandelions in the collapsing winds of our flailing ecologies, we shall inseminate the cybernetic state with entropic decay, bitter medicine, and the roar of the earth rising against domination. we are datura within the belly of the beast, incessant wildflowers creating the conditions ripe for imminent attack against all domination. welcome, make yourself at home and have fun cutting yourselves from the rotting corpse of colonial piety and the tremors of capitalistic death cults.

title: Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları: “Hakikat olmadan kalıcı barış olmaz”
content:
Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları, 1115’inci hafta buluşmasını bugün (8 Ağustos) İstanbul’daki Galatasaray Meydanı’nda gerçekleştirdi.


Kayıp yakınları ve hak savunucuları, kaybedilenlerin fotoğrafları ve karanfillerle meydana çıktı.


Haftanın basın açıklamasını İnsan Hakları Derneği (İHD) Kayıplar Komisyonu üyesi Sebla Arcan okudu.


Arcan: “Geçmişteki ağır hak ihlalleriyle yüzleşilmeli”


Sebla Arcan, devam eden Barış ve Demokratik Toplum Süreci’nin yalnızca ceza hukukuna ilişkin düzenlemelerle sınırlı kalmaması gerektiğini söyledi.


Kalıcı barış için geçmişte yaşanan ağır hak ihlalleriyle yüzleşmenin ve hak ihlaline uğrayanların adalet taleplerinin karşılanmasının gerekli olduğunu belirten Arcan, sürece “hakikat, adalet, onarım ve bir daha tekrarlamama” mekanizmalarının eşlik etmesini istedi.


Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları’nın taleplerini sıralayan Arcan, hakikat komisyonlarının kurulmasını, hakikati bilme hakkının yasal güvenceye alınmasını, zorla kaybetmelerde cezasızlığın sona erdirilmesini ve devlet arşivlerinin açılmasını istedi.


Arcan, “Hakikat olmadan adalet, adalet olmadan kalıcı barış olmaz” dedi.


Cumartesi Anneleri: Hiçbir çocuk babasının akıbetini bilmeden büyümemeli


1 Ağustos 2026


“Süleyman Cihan’a ne oldu?”


Bu haftaki buluşmada, 29 Temmuz 1981’de gözaltına alınan Süleyman Cihan’ın akıbeti ve dosyasındaki cezasızlık yeniden gündeme getirildi.


Arcan’ın aktardığına göre Cihan, Edirne’den İstanbul’a giderken bulunduğu otobüsün sivil polisler tarafından durdurulmasının ardından gözaltına alındı.


Önce Sansaryan Han’a, ardından Gayrettepe’deki emniyet birimine götürüldüğü belirtilen Cihan için ailesi ve avukatları emniyete ve savcılığa başvurdu. Ancak yetkililer, Cihan’ın gözaltına alınmadığını söyledi.


Daha sonra Cihan’ı gözaltında ve işkence altında gördüklerini söyleyen tanıklar ortaya çıktı.


45 yıldır soruyoruz: Süleyman Cihan’a ne oldu?

#CumartesiAnneleri1115Hafta


https://t.co/aJ0tNi15Eb


— Cumartesi Anneleri (@CmrtesiAnneleri)

August 8, 2026


Ölümüne “intihar” denildi


Arcan, Cihan’ın ölümüne ilişkin resmi açıklamaların zaman içinde değiştiğini söyledi.


Önce bir çatışmada öldüğünün öne sürüldüğünü, ardından altıncı kattaki bir daireden atlayarak intihar ettiği iddiasının gündeme getirildiğini aktardı.


Ancak Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları’nın açıklamasına göre otopsi raporunda Cihan’ın yüksekten düşmeden önce öldüğüne işaret eden bulgular yer alıyordu.


Açıklamada ayrıca olayla ilgili raporun 30 Temmuz 1981 tarihini taşımasına karşın, bu tarihten sonra Cihan’ı emniyette gördüğünü söyleyen tanıkların bulunduğu belirtildi.


1107. HAFTA


Cumartesi Anneleri/İnsanları: Veysel Güney’in mezar yerini açıklayın


13 Haziran 2026


“Cezasızlık hakikatin üzerini örtüyor”


Ailenin, avukatların ve tanıkların 85 gün süren arayışının ardından Cihan’ın cenazesinin Zindanarkası Mezarlığı’nın kimsesizler bölümünde “kimliği meçhul” olarak gömüldüğünün ortaya çıktığı belirtildi.


Sebla Arcan, Cihan’ın dosyasını cezasızlık politikasının sonuçlarından biri olarak değerlendirdi.


Cezasızlığın yalnızca failleri korumadığını, aynı zamanda hakikatin ortaya çıkmasını ve mağdurların adalete erişimini engellediğini söyleyen Arcan, aradan geçen zamana rağmen adalet talebinden vazgeçmeyeceklerini vurguladı.


Ahmet Cihan: “Failler açıkta, adaletin tecelli etmesi gerekiyor”


Süleyman Cihan’ın kardeşi Ahmet Cihan da Galatasaray Meydanı’ndaki açıklamada konuştu.


Kardeşinin dosyasında adı geçen ve haklarında delil bulunduğunu söylediği kişilerin devlet görevlileri olduğunu belirten Cihan, cezasızlık sürdüğü müddetçe meydanda olmaya devam edeceklerini söyledi.


“Failler açıkta, suç sabit” diyen Ahmet Cihan, adalet talebini yineledi.


1115’inci hafta buluşması, kaybedilenlerin anısına Galatasaray Meydanı’na karanfiller bırakılmasıyla sona erdi.


Yazar Burhan Sönmez de destek verdi

content:
dragon-in-a-fez

:

actually I think you should be normal about ordinary citizens of authoritarian countries and yes that applies even to that country you’re thinking of right now

In a individual sense: it heavily depends on their level of complicity in the state apparatus committing the atrocities, their ability to impact the composition of their government and the intensity of oppression they would face if they actively resisted the atrocities.

An 'ordinary’ American of European citizen has way more space to resist - and therefore way more of a duty to do so - than an ordinary Iranian citizen.

title: Eren: Democratisation steps must be taken after framework law
content:
The “Bill on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration,” prepared as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, has been submitted to the Presidency of the Grand National Assembly of Turkey.


Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM) Amed MP Serhat Eren spoke to ANF about the Framework Law.


How will the framework law be implemented?


First of all, it is useful to clarify this issue. This bill was first discussed by the Justice Commission. After that, it was approved and then brought before Parliament. The process will be completed by Monday at the latest. After it passes Parliament, the President will approve it, and it will be published in the Official Gazette. Once it has been published in the Official Gazette, there are two important points.


First, the two bodies specified in the law will be established immediately. One of these bodies will be established within the Presidency, namely a coordination office. This coordination office will include the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of National Defence, the General Secretariat of the National Security Council, the General Secretariat of the Presidency, the National Intelligence Organisation (MİT) and the relevant institutions.


Second, a commission will be established within Parliament. Subcommissions may also be established if necessary. The process of establishing these commissions will begin as soon as the law enters into force.


What steps will be taken regarding returns and releases?


PRISONS:


The National Security Council will prepare a report. It will say: “Yes, we have verified it. The weapons have been laid down.” The PKK has dissolved itself and the process of laying down arms will have been completed. The law will enter into force once the relevant report is published in the Official Gazette.


A six-month period will begin from the date on which the National Security Council’s report is published in the Official Gazette. During this six-month period, the process will apply to approximately 3,900 people in prison. Around 900 people will remain in prison. These will be people who have received aggravated life sentences and those who have been involved in killings from 2005 to the present. Everyone else currently in prison will be released.


EXILES:


Those abroad will also be able to apply directly. The person will apply either personally or through a lawyer. They will say, “I will return under this law; I will return to the country.” If their case is at the prosecution stage, the prosecutor’s office will immediately examine the file. It will examine it and say: “Yes, your case falls within the scope of this law. You can benefit from this law and return.”


There are also some people who are considered exceptions under this law. Regarding them, the prosecutor’s office will probably say, “You do not fall within the scope of this law,” or “Your situation falls under the provision defined as an exception, so you cannot benefit from it.” Consequently, they will not return either.


But I can say that 90 percent of those concerned will fall within the scope of the law. A person abroad will apply through their lawyer and will be informed that they can benefit from this law. When they return, they will simply submit their application and the case against them, if it is at the investigation stage, will be postponed.


Of course, when postponing the case, the prosecutor’s office will examine what the allegation in the investigation concerns. If the offence alleged corresponds to a crime for which the Turkish Penal Code prescribes a sentence of more than 15 years, the case will be postponed for 10 years. If it is an offence carrying a sentence of less than 15 years, the case will be postponed for five years. Unless an offence has been committed under the Anti-Terror Law — I am not referring to other ordinary offences, such as traffic accidents — the case will be dropped at the end of five or 10 years.


For those who have been sentenced, or rather those whose cases are before the Court of Cassation or an appeals court, the process will work differently. For detained people whose cases are before the Court of Cassation, the Court of Cassation will directly review their detention status, order their release and send the case back to the local court.

author: dialogocomospovos
title: A Comuna Amarildo de Souza: Teto, Terra e Território em Santa Catarina
content:
Santa Catarina não é feita apenas por aqueles que tentam apagar sua história de luta. O estado teve Anita Garibaldi, Antonieta de Barros, Cruz e Souza e tantos outros lutadores que construíram uma trajetória de resistência. É nesse espírito que nasce a Comuna Amarildo de Souza, um projeto de reforma agrária que prova que a luta por terra e território está viva e potente em solo catarinense.


Tudo começou em 16 de dezembro de 2013, quando 60 famílias cortaram as cercas de uma área de 900 hectares às margens da SC 401, em Florianópolis. A terra, grilada durante a ditadura militar pelo ex-deputado Artêmio Paludo, não cumpria sua função social enquanto milhares de famílias não tinham onde morar. A ocupação cresceu rapidamente: em uma semana já eram 250 famílias, chegando a 750 ao final de quatro meses, desafiando a especulação imobiliária no "coração do turismo" da capital.


Após despejos, negociações e muita resistência, em julho de 2014 o INCRA destinou às famílias uma área em Águas Mornas. Ali, contra todas as dificuldades, nasceu o primeiro assentamento na modalidade Projeto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (PDS) de Santa Catarina, com três pilares fundamentais: terra de uso coletivo, produção 100% agroecológica e decisões horizontais em assembleia.


Hoje, a Comuna produz mais de 50 itens agroecológicos, distribuídos semanalmente através de Células de Consumo Consciente em 15 pontos da Grande Florianópolis. Além disso, destinam cerca de 10% da produção para doações a cozinhas comunitárias, ocupações urbanas, comunidades indígenas e quilombolas. Durante a pandemia, doaram aproximadamente 3 toneladas de alimentos.


A agroecologia praticada na Comuna é popular e indissociável da reforma agrária. Como dizem os assentados: "enquanto existir latifúndio no Brasil, todos nós somos sem terra". A produção é da classe trabalhadora para a classe trabalhadora, construindo soberania alimentar, energética e hídrica, e apresentando um modelo capaz de substituir a lógica exploradora do agronegócio.


Após 12 anos de luta, a Comuna Amarildo de Souza segue firme, provando que é possível reflorestar, produzir comida saudável e construir um novo paradigma de organização social em Santa Catarina. A semente plantada em 2013 germinou e continua se espalhando.

author: Martha Teodoro
title: Senior citizens endure long wait for promised support
content:
Her experience reflects a fundamental question: Are senior citizens, especially centenarians, actually receiving the support promised to them?

MANILA – Nita Gonzaga, 85, thought all she had to do was wait.

The labor leader from San Andres, Manila had already submitted everything required for the government’s cash incentive for older Filipinos including her birth certificate, a valid ID and a photograph. No medical records. No income certification. The barangay officials handling the process are also senior citizens who know the community well which should hasten the process.

She said that barangay officials collected the documents months ago. But up to now, she has not received the P10,000 (US$164.46) cash gift promised under Republic Act No. 11982 (Expanded Centenarians Act). In fact, she said that none of the members of their senior citizens’ association in Barangay 738 had received this benefit.

Her experience reflects a fundamental question: Are senior citizens, especially centenarians, actually receiving the support promised to them?

For the past three decades, Congress has enacted measures expanding benefits for older Filipinos. Republic Act No. 9994 (Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010) grants senior citizens discounts and tax exemptions on medicines, healthcare, transportation and other essential goods and services. Meanwhile, Republic Act No. 10645 signed into law in November 2014 automatically enrolls all senior citizens in PhilHealth.

Approved in July 2022, Republic Act No. 11916 increased the monthly social pension for indigent senior citizens from P500 to P1,000 ($8.23 to $16.46). And more recently, Republic Act No. 11982 approved in February 2024 expanded government recognition of centenarians by providing P10,000 ($ 164.61) cash gifts to Filipinos upon reaching ages 80, 85, 90 and 95, while retaining the P100,000 ($1,464.09) incentive for those who reach 100 years old.

The expansion of these programs comes as the country’s elderly population continues to increase.

The Philippine Statistics Authority’s 2024 Census of Population reported that the country had 11.42 million senior citizens, representing 10.2 percent of the household population. During roughly the same period, for the May 2022 elections, the Commission on Elections (Comelec) reported about 11.47 million registered senior citizen voters.

According to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), around 4.1 million indigent senior citizens were receiving the Social Pension Program. For its part, the National Commission of Senior Citizens (NCSC) announced that 9.454 million had registered to receive their social benefits. Approximately 75,922 beneficiaries are under the Expanded Centenarians Act.

The PSA estimates the total senior citizen population, Comelec counts registered senior voters, the DSWD tracks social pension beneficiaries, and the NCSC monitors recipients of longevity incentives. These data point to a longstanding challenge raised by advocates and researchers that government agencies continue to maintain fragmented records of older Filipinos.

Judy Taguiwalo, a former DSWD secretary who also taught at the University of the Philippines, said that fragmented data have been the government’s persistent weakness. “Penetration ay isang problema. Ang veracity na information regarding the status of senior citizens,” she said. (Penetration is a problem. And the veracity of information regarding the status of senior citizens.)

She said that the separate databases maintained by local government units, DSWD, NCSC, and other agencies create inconsistencies that can lead to inclusion and exclusion errors in government programs. Some senior citizens appear in one database but not another while others experience delays because records have yet to be validated.

Republic Act No. 11982 attempted to address this problem. Aside from expanding cash gifts for milestone birthdays, the law directed the NCSC to establish an Elderly Data Management System in coordination with the Philippine Statistics Authority, DSWD, Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), and local government units. The system was intended to maintain an integrated database of older persons and beneficiaries, thus improving coordination among agencies and facilitating the implementation of programs. However, the different government statistics indicate that creating a cohesive national overview of the country’s senior citizens is still an …

author: Unknown
title: Armed groups issue threats as deadline expires; Iraqi authorities on alert
content:
Last week, the United States and Saudi Arabia carried out strikes against Hashd al-Shaabi (Popular Mobilization Forces) positions in several Iraqi provinces. The attacks killed 20 fighters and injured 32 others. In response, armed groups in Iraq issued threats, announcing that they would wait until the Arbaeen commemorations of Imam Husseinhad concluded, and that if the Iraqi government failed to respond, they would retaliate themselves.


The deadline set by the armed groups expires today. In a video released by one of the groups, armed men declared: “Listen, Saudis, your time is up. Prepare yourselves. Get your vehicles and equipment ready for rescue. We swear by the Kaaba that we will not rest until we have made you suffer even more.”


Following these threats, the Iraqi Joint Operations Command and security forces held an emergency meeting last night. There are concerns that the armed groups may launch an attack against Saudi Arabia. Several Iraqi officials have called on the groups to exercise restraint and postpone any military action.


In a video message, Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Fatah Alliance, called on fighters of the Islamic Resistance (Meqawmey Îslamî) to postpone any response to the U.S. and Saudi attacks. Al-Amiri urged the resistance forces to act responsibly, preserve stability in line with Iraq’s higher national interests, delay any attacks, and seek justice for the victims through diplomatic means.


Meanwhile, Kazım Fertusi, spokesperson for Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada, told Rojnews that the Islamic Resistance has so far been waiting to see what measures the Iraqi government will take in response to the Saudi strikes against Hashd al-Shaabi.


The Iraqi government is seeking to keep the armed groups under control by any means necessary and to prevent any attack from being launched from Iraqi territory. Officials are concerned about the consequences, fearing that such an incident could draw Iraq into a major war with unpredictable consequences.


According to security sources, Hashd al-Shaabi officials and the Iraqi government intervened this morning to prevent an attack on a Saudi port. Following the intervention, the Islamic Resistance group decided to postpone its planned retaliation.


Meanwhile, the newspaper Okaz, citing official Saudi sources, reported that intelligence assessments indicate coordination between the Houthis, Iraqi armed groups, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in preparing for a potential attack against Saudi Arabia.

author: Unknown
title: MP Celal Fırat: Alevis want a Turkey where everyone’s rights are guaranteed
content:
With the framework law, a new phase begins in the peace and democratic society process in Turkey. In an interview with ANF, DEM Party MP Celal Fırat explained the expectations of the Alevi community regarding this process. According to Fırat, peace can only be lasting if it is built on democracy, the rule of law, and the equal participation of all segments of society.


Peace is a historical experience for Alevis


According to Fırat, peace holds a special significance for Alevis. He said that the community has endured centuries of discrimination, persecution, and massacres, and therefore welcomes every genuine initiative aimed at achieving a peaceful solution. The silence of weapons, mothers no longer losing their children, and young people experiencing a future instead of war are shared aspirations. However, he emphasized that peace means far more than simply ending armed conflict.


“True peace means strengthening the rule of law, deepening democracy, and ensuring that every person can feel like an equal member of this country. If this process contributes not only to resolving a conflict but also to ushering in a new era of rights, justice, and equality, we will all benefit from it.”


Referring to the Alevi understanding of faith, Fırat pointed to the principle: “Even if you are wronged, do not wrong anyone.”


He said that peace means building a shared future in which no one loses and everyone can live in freedom.


Trust is built through transparency


According to Fırat, many Alevis view the current process with hope, but also with caution. He stressed that this caution does not reflect opposition to peace, but rather the result of historical experience.


“Throughout history, Alevis have repeatedly experienced that promises made to them were not kept. Therefore, we expect this process to be conducted not behind closed doors, but on the basis of parliamentary decisions, the rule of law, transparent procedures, and public participation.”


Fırat said that peace can only be lasting if no one feels excluded from the search for a solution.


“We do not oppose the rights of others. On the contrary, we want a Turkey where the rights of everyone are guaranteed. If any community feels excluded, it will be difficult to build lasting peace.”


Peace and equal rights go hand in hand


According to Fırat, the Alevi community will continue to support the peace process while also maintaining its own democratic demands. These include the legal recognition of Cemevis (Alevi place of worship), unrestricted freedom of religion, and full equality for Alevis. He stressed that these demands are not in conflict with the peace process, but are instead an integral part of a democratic society based on equal rights.


“We want a country where no mother has to bury her child anymore, and no child grows up in fear because of their identity or faith. True peace is achieved when all people can feel equal, safe, and live with dignity.”


In closing, Fırat reaffirmed that the Alevi community will continue to stand on the side of peace, democracy, and human dignity. He said that the words of the Alevi scholar Hacı Bektaş Veli continue to serve as a guiding principle:


“Let us be united, let us be great, and let us be alive.”

title: Sebahat Tuncel: Together, we will build a democratic life
content:
The 58th Tatvan Culture and Arts Festival, held under the slogan “There is culture in Tatvan, there is art in Tatvan, we are here,” continued with its eighth day of events in Tatvan district of Bitlis.


As part of the program, the Free Women’s Movement (Tevgera Jinên Azad – TJA) organized a press statement beside Nemrut Crater Lake to draw attention to the destruction of women and nature. The event was attended by TJA activist Sebahat Tuncel, representatives of political parties and democratic organizations in the city, as well as numerous women.


Addressing the crowd here, Sebahat Tuncel said the following:


“The issue is not only to oppose the destruction of our nature; it is also about embracing an ecological perspective while building a free future. Ecology is not merely about protecting the environment—it is a way of life and a philosophy. In the coming period, ecology may well become the issue we discuss most. As human beings, an approach and a system that ignores nature and considers every form of domination and exploitation of it to be legitimate is destroying the natural world we live in today. If we are experiencing such a severe climate crisis and ecological destruction has reached such profound levels, it is because of the mindset that sees nature as a source of profit and exploitation. The resources of nature are sufficient for everyone.


The exploitation of women is connected to the exploitation of nature. As women, while we carry forward the struggle for women’s freedom, we also oppose the oppression of nature. Together, we will build a democratic life.”

author: Unknown
title: Murder of Musa Anter: Family files a request to reopen the case
content:
The family of Kurdish journalist and writer Musa Anter, who was killed in 1992 by the Turkish military intelligence unit JITEM, has filed a request to reopen the case. Rahşan Yorozlu, Anter’s daughter, submitted the application through her lawyer Bişar Abdi Alinak to the Department for the Investigation of Unsolved Crimes at the Turkish Ministry of Justice. The aim is to reopen the proceedings, which were dismissed in 2022 due to the statute of limitations. The application calls for a comprehensive reassessment of the case and further investigations to ensure that all those responsible for the killing are held criminally accountable.


New investigation and modern forensic analysis requested


In the application, the family requests that previously omitted investigative measures be carried out and that all evidence collected in the case be reexamined using current forensic and criminal investigation techniques. The applicants also demand a full clarification of the crime and investigations into everyone involved throughout the chain of command. The stated objective is to fully establish the circumstances of the murder and determine the criminal responsibility of all those involved.


Decades without an effective investigation


Musa Anter was murdered on September 20, 1992, in Amed (Diyarbakır). Former JITEM operative Abdülkadir Aygan later stated that Anter had been killed by a unit of which he himself had been a member. Despite this, no effective investigation was carried out for years. It was only after the family brought the case before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), which found violations of the right to life in both its substantive and procedural aspects, that the proceedings were reopened. In 2009, 17 years after the murder, the Special Prosecutor’s Office in Amed launched a new investigation based on Aygan’s testimony.


Case dismissed despite confessions


Shortly before the statute of limitations was due to expire, state witness Hamit Yıldırım was arrested in June 2012. A year later, prosecutors indicted Hamit Yıldırım, alleged JITEM operative Mahmut Yıldırım, known by the codename “Yeşil,” Abdülkadir Aygan, and retired Colonel Savaş Gevrekçi on charges of premeditated murder and other offenses.


In 2015, the case was transferred from Amed to Ankara on security grounds, where it was merged with the so-called main JITEM trial. On September 21, 2022, Ankara’s 6th High Criminal Court dismissed the case on the grounds that the statute of limitations had expired.


With the newly submitted application, the family is making a renewed legal effort to fully clarify the murder of Musa Anter and to hold those responsible accountable, despite the dismissal of the original proceedings.

title: MHP’s Fethi Yıldız reads Öcalan’s February 27 call at parliamentary committee session
content:
The “Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Cohesion,” prepared as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process and submitted to the Speaker of Parliament on August 5 with the signatures of 360 MPs, is being discussed in the Parliamentary Justice Committee.


The committee session began with opening remarks by Justice Committee Chair Cüneyt Yüksel, followed by a presentation of the bill by the ruling AKP Deputy Chair Abdulhamit Gül.


Speaking afterward, MHP (Nationalist Movement Party) Deputy Chair Fethi Yıldız shared his assessment of the proposal. Recalling MHP Chair Devlet Bahçeli’s earlier call to Abdullah Öcalan, Yıldız said that a new era has begun in Turkish politics.


During his speech, Yıldız read Öcalan’s “Call for Peace and Democratic Society” issued on February 27, 2025, and recalled that the PKK dissolved itself after the call.


Yıldız continued: “Weapons were burned in a ceremony. That marked a new phase, followed by the establishment of the parliamentary committee. Now a temporary law has been prepared. The law is important for unity and does not open the way to amnesty or impunity. It also includes the verification and documentation of the surrender of weapons and military inventories. This temporary law will strengthen the rule of law in Turkey. As the MHP, we are committed to safeguarding the brotherhood that has existed for thousands of years. Our Kurdish brothers and sisters are an integral part of the Turkish nation. We do not want to carry any more coffins on our shoulders.”


At times, the committee’s deliberations were interrupted by heated exchanges and arguments.

title: Turkish national on wanted list appointed division commander in Syria
content:
The Syrian transitional authorities have appointed Turkish national Ömer Muhammed Çiftçi as commander of the 62nd Division.


The appointment has drawn attention because of the agreement reached on January 29 between the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and the transitional government, which provides for the removal of non-Syrian fighters from the country.


Born in Osmaniye, Turkey, in 1980, Ömer Muhammed Çiftçi operated under the aliases Muhtar Türki and Umar Mohammed Jaftashi. He joined al-Qaeda in Afghanistan in 2004 and later traveled to Syria in 2012, where he joined the HTS (Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham).


Çiftçi had previously been included on Turkey’s Ministry of Interior’s most wanted list because of his alleged links to al-Qaeda. Ankara removed him from the wanted list after HTS came to power in Syria in December 2024.
